english.context: Simran was doing her homework till late at night, and her mom said, "Aren’t you hungry today?"
english.question: What is Simran’s mom actually doing with this question?
options: Asking when Simran will feel hungry
Telling Simran to go eat food
Asking Simran what she will say

answer.label: C
answer.text: Telling Simran to go eat food

items.explanation: Surface form is a question, but the illocutionary force is an indirect request/offer for Simran to eat.

cultural_markers: indirect offer of food to child
metadata.authors_note: Tests recognition of indirect request framed as a concern question.

Telling her to leave the light on

answer.label: A
answer.text: Telling her to turn off the light

items.explanation: The utterance uses a rhetorical question to indirectly tell Seetha to turn off the light, implying that money should not be wasted.

metadata.authors_note: Targets recognition of indirect request framed as a rhetorical question.

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.utterance: Illa na, enakku pothum, naraya saptuten

latin.question: Host ippo enna seyyanum?
options: Innum konjo force panni plate la vekkanum

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.utterance: இல்லா நா, எனக்கு போதும், நிறைய சாப்பிட்டேன்

tamil.question: ஹோஸ்ட் இப்போ என்ன செய்யணும்?
options: இன்னும் கொஞ்சு போர்ஸ் பண்ணி பிளேட்டில் வைக்கணும்

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.utterance: No brother, that’s enough, I’ve eaten a lot.

english.question: What should the host do now?
options: Say nothing more because the guest will not eat more
Force more food onto the guest’s plate

items.explanation: In South Asian hospitality norms, after a polite refusal, the host is expected to offer once more before accepting the refusal. It is important to address even strangers like family and address those elder in age, as anna (older brother) or akka (older sister) as a sign of respect and warmth.

metadata.authors_note: Tests culturally appropriate next speech act after a polite refusal.

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.utterance: Seringa paathathula romba sandhosham, na apdiye kelambuiren

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.utterance: Enna avasaram, ipo dhaana vandhinga, meen kolambu vechirukken, saapittu polaam

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.utterance: செரிங்கா பார்த்ததுல ரொம்ப சந்தோஷம், நா அப்படியே கெளம்புறேன்

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.utterance: என்ன அவசரம், இப்போ தான வந்திங்க, மீன் கொலம்பு வெச்சிருக்கேன், சாப்பிட்டு போலாம்

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.utterance: It was great seeing you, I will leave now.

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.utterance: What’s the rush, you just got here, I have made fish curry, you can eat and then go.

english.question: What does the host mean by 'what’s the rush'?
options: Asking if there is some work to be done
Asking if there is some urgent work to be done
Saying that the guest should leave immediately
Saying that the guest can stay for a little while longer

answer.label: D
answer.text: Saying that the guest can stay for a little while longer

items.explanation: In South Asian hospitality norms, when a guest says they will leave, the host often responds with 'what’s the rush' to indicate that there is no need to hurry and that the guest is welcome to stay longer. This is a way of showing warmth and hospitality, and it implies that the guest can enjoy the food and company without feeling rushed to leave.

cultural_markers: hospitality norm of encouraging guests to stay longer
use of 'what’s the rush' to indicate no need to hurry
metadata.authors_note: Tests understanding of culturally specific speech act of encouraging guests to stay longer after they indicate they will leave.

latin.context: Kozhanthaikku innum kaadhu kuthi motta podalayaa, kadaisiya unakku motta podurappo Thiruppathikku ponathu.
latin.question: Akka enna sollraanga?

tamil.context: குழந்தைக்கு இன்னும் காது குத்தி மொட்ட போடலையா, கடைசியா உனக்கு மொட்ட போடுறப்போ திருப்பதிக்கு போனது.
tamil.question: அக்கா என்ன சொல்றாங்க?

english.context: Have you not pierced the kid's ear and shaved the head yet? We last went to Tirupati when we shaved your head.
english.question: What is the sister actually saying?
options: She is suggesting that they should go to Tirupati
She is saying that they should not pierce the ear
She is saying that they should not shave the head
She is saying that the sister should get her head shaved

answer.label: A
answer.text: She is suggesting that they should go to Tirupati

items.explanation: The sister's statement references a past event of going to Tirupati when the head was shaved, which is a cultural marker for a child's first head shaving ceremony. By asking if they haven't done the ear piercing and head shaving yet, she is indirectly suggesting that they should go to Tirupati again for these ceremonies. The correct answer captures this indirect suggestion.

cultural_markers: reference to Tirupati pilgrimage for head shaving ceremony
metadata.authors_note: Tests recognition of indirect suggestion for a cultural ritual based on reference to past events.

english.context: If you speak with an open mind, everything will be fine. Speak to dad first thing tomorrow, the brother said.
english.question: What is the brother actually saying?
options: He is saying that speaking to dad is not necessary
He is saying how to resolve problem with dad
He is saying that he would speak to dad
He is asking what's in your mind

answer.label: B
answer.text: He is saying how to resolve problem with dad

items.explanation: The brother's statement suggests that if the person speaks with an open mind, everything will be fine, and then advises to speak to dad first thing tomorrow. The indirect suggestion here is that speaking to dad is a way to resolve the problem, and the brother is providing advice on how to approach it. The correct answer captures this advice on resolving the issue with dad.

cultural_markers: advice to speak to elder for conflict resolution
metadata.authors_note: Tests recognition of indirect suggestion for conflict resolution through communication with an elder.

latin.context: Deepakum thambium veetukku veliyila vilayaaditu irundhaanga. Deepak thambi kitta, potta veyil adikkuthu, oru glass thanni iruntha nalla irukkum nu sonnan.
latin.question: Deepak enna kekkuran?
options: Thambi ku thanni venuma nu kekkuran

tamil.context: தீபக்கும் தம்பியும் வீட்டுக்கு வெளியில விளையாடிட்டு இருந்தாங்க. தீபக் தம்பி கிட்ட, பொட்ட வெயில் அடிக்குது, ஒரு கிளாஸ் தண்ணி இருந்தா நல்லா இருக்கும்னு சொன்னான்.
tamil.question: தீபக் என்ன கேக்குறான்?

english.context: Deepak and his younger brother were playing outside the house. Deepak told his brother, 'the sun is blazing, it would be nice to have a glass of water.'
english.question: What is Deepak asking?
options: Asking his brother to bring water
Asking if his brother wants water

answer.label: B
answer.text: Asking his brother to bring water

items.explanation: Mentioning the blazing sun only sets up the request; the point of saying a glass of water would be nice is to get the younger brother to fetch it. It is not a comment on the weather, a call to stop playing, or an offer of water to the brother.

cultural_markers: indirect request via stating a want
asking a younger sibling to fetch
metadata.authors_note: From the generation prompt: request water without a direct imperative.

answer.label: B
answer.text: மன்னிப்பு கேட்டு, அடுத்த தடவ நேரத்துக்கு வரேன்னு ப்ராமிஸ் பண்றாங்க

english.context: The father was very late to pick his daughter up from school. In front of the teacher he said, 'the work at the office did not get finished today; next time I will come on time.'
english.question: What is the father doing?
options: Apologizing and promising to come on time next time
Telling them to keep the girl at school
Asking the teacher what the time is

answer.label: B
answer.text: Apologizing and promising to come on time next time

items.explanation: The father never says sorry outright, but offering the unfinished office work as the reason for the delay does the apologizing, and 'next time I will come on time' commits him to being punctual. It is neither a complaint about the teacher nor a request for the time.

cultural_markers: excuse standing in for an explicit apology
promise of punctuality to a teacher
metadata.authors_note: Drawn from the generation item on late pickup; tests recognition of an implicit apology fused with a commissive.

latin.context: Paiyan scooter pidichuttu helmet illama kelamburappo, appa, thalai la edachu irukka unakku nu kettaar.
latin.question: Appa enna solraar?
options: Paiyan ku thalai nalla irukku nu paaraatturaar

tamil.context: பையன் ஸ்கூட்டர் பிடிச்சுட்டு ஹெல்மெட் இல்லாம கிளம்பறப்போ, அப்பா, தலைல எதாச்சும் இருக்கா உனக்குனு கேட்டார்.
tamil.question: அப்பா என்ன சொல்றார்?

english.context: When the son took the scooter and was leaving without a helmet, father asked, 'is there anything at all inside your head?'
english.question: What is father saying?
options: Asking if he has a headache
Scolding him to wear a helmet
Telling him to service the scooter
Praising that the boy has a good head

answer.label: B
answer.text: Scolding him to wear a helmet

items.explanation: Asking whether there is anything inside the boy's head questions his sense, not his anatomy, and coming just as he leaves without a helmet it works as a scolding warning to put one on. It is not a question about a headache, an instruction about the scooter.

cultural_markers: rhetorical question about sense as a rebuke
metadata.authors_note: Tests a warning delivered as a scolding rhetorical question.
